kurals.tamil:
யாதனின் யாதனின் நீங்கியான் நோதல்
அதனின் அதனின் இலன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Yaadhanin yaadhanin neengiyaan nodhal
Adhanin adhanin ilan.
kurals.meaning: Whatever thing a person has freed himself from — whatever it may be — from that very thing he suffers no more pain.
kurals.elementary: If you stop caring about keeping a certain toy, you won't cry when it breaks. This kural says every single thing you stop clinging to is one less thing that can make you sad.
kurals.university: The doubled pronouns (yaadhanin yaadhanin … adhanin adhanin, “from whatever, whatever … from that, that”) set up an exact one-to-one ledger: each object released cancels the suffering tied to that particular object. Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as the gradualist justification for renunciation — one need not abandon everything at once to begin reaping relief, since each detachment pays its own dividend; Karunanidhi likewise glosses it as “whichever single attachment one gives up.” The chapter therefore opens not with an ascetic command but with a near-empirical observation about the mechanics of grief: pain travels along the line of attachment. The same causal claim underlies the Buddhist analysis of suffering as arising from clinging (upādāna) and the Stoic insistence that distress comes from our relation to externals rather than from the externals themselves.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who neither hates nor desires the fruits of his activities is known to be always renounced. Such a person, liberated from all dualities, easily overcomes material bondage and is completely liberated, O mighty-armed Arjuna.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna defines the true renunciate not by outward robes but by an inner state: someone who neither craves nor resents outcomes, and who therefore slips easily out of bondage.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says what you have let go of can no longer hurt you; the Gita says the one who no longer craves is freed from the bondage that craving creates.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual match (non-craving yields freedom from bondage/pain); the Gita frames it around fruits of action rather than possessions.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that earthly treasure is always exposed to decay and theft, and urges his hearers to invest where nothing can be lost.
christianity.tie_back: Both locate vulnerability in what we hold: release the earthly treasure and moth, rust and thief lose their power to wound you.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on 'what you hold is what can hurt you'; Jesus redirects attachment to heaven rather than simply dissolving it.

islam.quote_or_event: “In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you. And Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful -”
islam.explanation: The Quran teaches that events are decreed so that believers neither collapse over what they lose nor grow proud over what they gain.
islam.tie_back: The same equanimity the Kural describes: loss cannot wound a person whose heart is not bound to the thing lost.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on the psychological outcome (no despair at loss); the Quran grounds it in divine decree rather than renunciation as a practice.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: Stripped in one day of his wealth and his children, Job answers that he arrived with nothing and will leave with nothing, and blesses God.
judaism.tie_back: Job's un-possessive stance lets him face catastrophic loss without collapse — the Kural's principle tested at its most extreme.
judaism._accuracy_note: Job still mourns (he tears his robe); the detachment is theological submission rather than chosen renunciation, so the match is partial.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces grief and fear directly to what we hold dear, and declares that one wholly free of such attachment has no grief at all.
buddhism.tie_back: Nearly identical logic to the Kural: grief follows attachment, so where attachment is removed, the grief tied to it is gone.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; verses 213-216 repeat the formula for affection, attachment, lust and craving.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “It would be absurd, if Manes can live without Diogenes, but Diogenes cannot get on without Manes.”
greek_mythology.explanation: When Diogenes the Cynic's slave Manes ran away and friends urged him to chase him, Diogenes refused with this reply.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Diogenes simply declines to let the loss hurt him, because he never made his contentment depend on Manes — the Kural's point made as a joke.
greek_mythology.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.55 (tr. R. D. Hicks)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match, but this is a Cynic biographical anecdote rather than myth proper; used because Greek myth offers no closer parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Never say of anything, "I have lost it"; but, "I have returned it." Is your child dead? It is returned. Is your wife dead? She is returned. Is your estate taken away? Well, and is not that likewise returned?”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus trains his students to treat everything external as on loan, so that its loss is experienced as a return rather than a theft.
philosophy.tie_back: Once a thing is no longer held as 'mine', its departure causes no pain — exactly the Kural's claim.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close match: non-possession of externals as the cure for grief at their loss.

kurals.tamil:
வேண்டின்உண் டாகத் துறக்க துறந்தபின்
ஈண்டுஇயற் பால பல.
kurals.transliteration:
Vendin undaagath thurakka thurandhapin
Eendu iyarpaala pala.
kurals.meaning: If you want lasting good, renounce while you still have things to renounce; once you have renounced, many joys become available even here in this life.
kurals.elementary: Taking a heavy backpack off before a long hike isn't losing anything — it's how you get to enjoy the walk. This kural says give things up while you still have them, and you'll find lots of happiness right away.
kurals.university: The phrase undaaga (“while [they] exist”) is read by Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan as a timing instruction: renounce while wealth, strength and opportunity are still in hand, not after they have already slipped away — giving up what one no longer has is not renunciation at all. The second line's eendu (“here”, in this world) is striking: Valluvar promises not only a post-mortem reward but many present goods (iyarpaala pala), countering the caricature of renunciation as pure deprivation. This anticipates the famous Upanishadic paradox that one enjoys by relinquishing. Placed after the Kural's earlier praise of the householder (ch. 5, Ilvaazhkai), the couplet presents thuravu as a voluntary, later-chosen stage rather than a universal command.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “All this, whatsoever moves on earth, is to be hidden in the Lord (the Self). When thou hast surrendered all this, then thou mayest enjoy. Do not covet the wealth of any man!”
hinduism.explanation: The opening verse of the Isha Upanishad teaches that the world belongs to the Lord, and that true enjoyment comes only after surrendering one's claim to it.
hinduism.tie_back: Same paradox as the Kural: renounce first, and then the joys follow — even in this life.
hinduism.source: Isha (Vajasaneyi-samhita) Upanishad 1 (tr. F. Max Müller, SBE vol. 1)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Excellent match on 'renounce, then enjoy'; the Kural adds the timing element (while you still possess).

christianity.quote_or_event: “There is no man that hath left house, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my sake, and the gospel’s, But he shall receive an hundredfold now in this time, houses, and brethren, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and lands, with persecutions; and in the world to come eternal life.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus promises those who leave everything for him a hundredfold return 'now in this time', as well as eternal life hereafter.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's eendu (here), Jesus insists the rewards of renunciation begin in this life, not only after death.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on present-life reward for renunciation; Mark adds 'with persecutions' and a Christocentric motive.

islam.quote_or_event: “Be indifferent towards this world, and Allah will love you. Be indifferent to what is in people’s hands, and they will love you.”
islam.explanation: Asked for a deed that would win the love of God and people, the Prophet recommends zuhd — detachment from worldly goods.
islam.tie_back: Zuhd brings concrete goods in return — divine and human love — echoing the Kural's promise of many joys after renouncing.
islam._accuracy_note: Thematically close; note that Darussalam grades this chain da'if (weak), though the hadith is widely circulated in Islamic ethical literature.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot, as it is said: ‘You shall enjoy the fruit of your labors, you shall be happy and you shall prosper’ (Psalms 128:2) ‘You shall be happy’ in this world, ‘and you shall prosper’ in the world to come.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines wealth as contentment, and reads the psalm as promising happiness in this world and prosperity in the next.
judaism.tie_back: Contentment rather than accumulation is the path to joy 'in this world' — close to the Kural's promise of joys 'here'.
judaism._accuracy_note: Rabbinic Judaism commends contentment, not renunciation of property; the match is on the result (joy here and hereafter) rather than the method.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If by renouncing a lesser happiness one may realize a greater happiness, let the wise man renounce the lesser, having regard for the greater.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha frames renunciation as a rational exchange: give up a smaller pleasure to gain a larger one.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's bargain — if you want the many joys, renounce.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-direct match on renunciation as the price of greater happiness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Crates of Thebes, born wealthy, is said to have turned his property into money and distributed it among his fellow citizens, then lived as a cheerful Cynic beggar-philosopher.
greek_mythology.explanation: According to Diogenes Laertius, Crates gave away a large inheritance and embraced the Cynic life, becoming known for his good humour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Crates renounced while he still had much to give up, and found joy in the renounced life — the Kural's timing and promise in one biography.
greek_mythology.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.87 (tr. R. D. Hicks)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a Cynic biographical tradition, not a myth; the details of his divestment vary between ancient accounts.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that wealth is measured by the limit of one's wants, not by the size of one's possessions.
philosophy.tie_back: Letting go of craving is what makes one rich — a Stoic version of the Kural's claim that renunciation brings many goods.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 2 (tr. R. M. Gummere)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Seneca advocates moderation of desire, not full renunciation; partial match.

kurals.tamil:
அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை விடல்வேண்டும்
வேண்டிய வெல்லாம் ஒருங்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Adalvendum aindhan pulaththai vidalvendum
Vendiya vellaam orungu.
kurals.meaning: One must subdue the five senses and, at the same time, give up together everything those senses crave.
kurals.elementary: Imagine five puppies each pulling you toward a different treat. You need to hold all five leashes AND put all the treats away. This kural says control all five senses and let go of everything they want, all at once.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on two parallel imperatives (adalvendum … vidalvendum, “must conquer … must abandon”): conquest of the five sense-fields (aindhan pulam — sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch) and the simultaneous relinquishing of all that they desire. The final word orungu (“together, all at once”) is decisive; Parimelazhagar stresses that a partial abandonment leaves a foothold from which desire regrows. Pairing inner control with outer relinquishment mirrors the Indic scheme of indriya-nigraha and tyaga, and recalls Kural 6's praise of the one who has quenched the five sense-gates. Across traditions the senses appear as the doorways through which the world lays claim to the self — the Gita's tortoise, Plato's unruly horse, Odysseus's wax-stopped crew.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is able to withdraw his senses from sense objects, as the tortoise draws his limbs within the shell, is to be understood as truly situated in knowledge.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna compares the steady sage to a tortoise that can pull all its limbs inside its shell at will.
hinduism.tie_back: The tortoise withdraws all its limbs together — the Kural's 'conquer the five senses' and 'orungu' (all at once) in a single image.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close match on sense-withdrawal; the Gita emphasises inner mastery more than outward abandonment of objects.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world. And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.”
christianity.explanation: John names the cravings of the body and the eyes as belonging to a passing world, and contrasts them with doing God's will.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts see sense-desire as the channel that binds us to the world, and call for turning away from it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good thematic match; John names flesh and eyes rather than a systematic five-sense scheme.

islam.quote_or_event: “But as for he who feared the position of his Lord and prevented the soul from [unlawful] inclination, Then indeed, Paradise will be [his] refuge.”
islam.explanation: The Quran promises Paradise to the one who restrains the self (nafs) from its unlawful desires out of reverence for God.
islam.tie_back: Restraint of the desiring self is the gateway to the highest state — parallel to the Kural's call to conquer the senses.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches on restraining desire; the Quran restricts this to unlawful inclination rather than all sense-desire.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: ‘He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city’ (Proverbs 16:32).”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines strength as the conquest of one's own impulses rather than of other people.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's 'adal' (conquest) is turned inward in exactly the same way: the real victory is over one's own desires.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches on self-conquest; Judaism aims at governing the yetzer (inclination), not abandoning all sense-objects.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Good is restraint over the eye; good is restraint over the ear; good is restraint over the nose; good is restraint over the tongue. Good is restraint in the body; good is restraint in speech; good is restraint in thought. Restraint everywhere is good. The monk restrained in every way is freed from all suffering.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists restraint over each sense in turn and concludes that total restraint frees the monk from suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: A sense-by-sense version of the Kural's command to conquer all five senses together.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-exact match, including the sense-by-sense enumeration and 'restraint everywhere'.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sailing past the Sirens, Odysseus stops his crew's ears with wax and has himself bound to the mast so their song cannot draw him to ruin.
greek_mythology.explanation: Warned by Circe, Odysseus uses physical restraint to overcome a sensory lure that has destroyed every sailor before him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Sirens personify the pull of sense-objects; blocking the senses entirely is how Odysseus survives — a mythic image of the Kural's command.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Moderate match; Odysseus still wants to hear the song, so it is restraint without inner renunciation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedrus, Socrates pictures the soul as a charioteer driving two horses, one noble and one unruly, and describes the struggle to rein in the unruly horse of appetite.
philosophy.explanation: Plato's allegory makes self-mastery a matter of reason forcibly controlling the appetites that pull toward sensual objects.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats the appetites as forces that must be conquered, not negotiated with.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; Plato's goal is ordered love of beauty rather than renunciation of all sense-objects.

kurals.tamil:
இயல்பாகும் நோன்பிற்கொன்று இன்மை உடைமை
மயலாகும் மற்றும் பெயர்த்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Iyalbaagum nonbirkondru inmai udaimai
Mayalaagum matrum peyarththu.
kurals.meaning: Owning nothing at all is the natural condition of true austerity; possessing even one thing turns a person back into the very delusion he had left behind.
kurals.elementary: If you are trying to stop eating sweets, keeping 'just one piece' in your pocket makes it very hard to stop thinking about sweets. This kural says someone who has given things up should keep nothing, because even one thing can pull them back.
kurals.university: Inmai (having nothing) is called the iyalbu — the natural, defining character — of nonbu (austerity, tapas). The second line's peyarththu (“turning back, reversing”) suggests that possession does not merely distract but undoes progress, returning the renunciant to mayal, bewilderment; Karunanidhi glosses that even one attachment multiplies into many. This is a stricter standard than Kural 341's gradualism, and it applies specifically to one who has already taken up the ascetic life. Comparable rules shaped the Buddhist monk's short list of requisites, the Jain ideal of aparigraha, and the apostolic mission charge in Matthew 10; the Cynic Diogenes made the same point theatrically.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Such a man of understanding acts with mind and intelligence perfectly controlled, gives up all sense of proprietorship over his possessions and acts only for the bare necessities of life. Thus working, he is not affected by sinful reactions.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the sage who has abandoned all possessiveness (tyakta-sarva-parigraha) and keeps only what bare survival needs.
hinduism.tie_back: Both identify non-possession as the defining mark of the renunciate.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on non-possession; the Gita focuses on proprietorship (the sense of 'mine') rather than the literal absence of things.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Provide neither gold, nor silver, nor brass in your purses, Nor scrip for your journey, neither two coats, neither shoes, nor yet staves: for the workman is worthy of his meat.”
christianity.explanation: Sending out the twelve apostles, Jesus forbids them to carry money, spare clothing or supplies.
christianity.tie_back: The missionary is to own nothing, like the Kural's ascetic, depending entirely on God and on others' hospitality.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close practical parallel; the command is a mission instruction rather than a permanent ascetic rule.

islam.quote_or_event: “Your wealth and your children are but a trial, and Allah has with Him a great reward.”
islam.explanation: The Quran describes possessions and family as a test that can distract the believer from God.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's warning that possession brings back delusion, the Quran treats wealth as a trial that can lead the heart astray.
islam._accuracy_note: Partial match: Islam treats wealth as a test to be handled rightly, not something to be abandoned (cf. Quran 57:27 on monasticism being a human innovation).

judaism.explanation: Hillel's saying lists the hidden costs that come with each kind of increase — including more worry with more possessions.
judaism.tie_back: Possession breeds a disturbed mind — a Jewish echo of the Kural's 'possession brings bewilderment'.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on the psychological cost of property; Avot does not ask one to own nothing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Happy indeed we live, we who possess nothing. Feeders on joy we shall be, like the Radiant Gods.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the monks' happiness as flowing from owning nothing at all.
buddhism.tie_back: Owning nothing is not a hardship but the natural condition of the joyful renunciate — the Kural's 'inmai' as 'iyalbu'.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close match on non-possession as the renunciate's natural state.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “A child has beaten me in plainness of living.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Seeing a child drink water from his cupped hands, Diogenes threw away the cup from his bag, saying this.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Even one small possession was one too many for Diogenes — the Kural's point that the ascetic should keep nothing.
greek_mythology.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.37 (tr. R. D. Hicks)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match; Cynic anecdote rather than myth, used because Greek myth has no closer parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For to that which once exceeds a due measure, there is no bound.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus warns that once one goes beyond what the body actually needs, desire has no natural stopping point — the shoe becomes gilded, then purple, then jewelled.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's 'possession brings delusion again', even one step beyond need restarts an endless cycle of wanting.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Epictetus allows possessions up to bodily need rather than owning nothing; partial match.

kurals.tamil:
மற்றும் தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல் பிறப்பறுக்கல்
உற்றார்க்கு உடம்பும் மிகை.
kurals.transliteration:
Matrum thodarppaadu evankol pirapparukkal
Utraarkku udambum migai.
kurals.meaning: For those who are striving to end the cycle of birth, even the body is one thing too many — so why take on any further ties?
kurals.elementary: If you are trying to swim across a river, even your shoes feel heavy. Why would you carry a suitcase too? This kural says someone trying to be truly free finds even their own body a load, so they shouldn't add extra burdens.
kurals.university: The couplet argues a fortiori: if even the body — the one attachment that cannot simply be discarded — is migai (excess, surplus) to someone who has set out to cut off births (pirappu arukkal), then every additional bond (thodarppaadu) is indefensible. Parimelazhagar notes that the body is retained only as the instrument through which austerity is practised, not valued for its own sake. The verse does not counsel harming the body; it relocates the body from 'self' to 'tool'. The idea resonates with Plato's Phaedo, where philosophy is a rehearsal for the soul's release from the body, with Paul's groaning 'in this tabernacle', and with the Buddha's house-builder verse, in which the body is the house craving keeps rebuilding.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When the embodied being is able to transcend these three modes, he can become free from birth, death, old age and their distresses and can enjoy nectar even in this life.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that the soul, by rising above the qualities that arise from the body, escapes the cycle of birth, death and ageing.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts aim at ending rebirth by loosening identification with the body and what grows from it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shared goal (ending birth) and body-transcendence; the Gita does not call the body 'excess' or argue from it to other ties.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened: not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes the present body as a tent in which believers groan under a burden while longing for a greater, immortal life.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul experiences the body itself as a burden for one set on a higher life.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches on the body as burden; Paul hopes for bodily transformation (resurrection), not escape from embodiment.

islam.quote_or_event: “Be in this world as if you were a stranger or a traveler.”
islam.explanation: Taking Ibn Umar by the shoulder, the Prophet told him to live in the world as a passing traveller, not a settler.
islam.tie_back: A traveller carries only what the road requires; the Kural likewise asks the seeker to add no ties beyond the bare vehicle of the journey.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on minimal attachment for one on a journey; the hadith concerns the world, not specifically the body.

judaism.quote_or_event: “This world is like a vestibule before the world to come; prepare yourself in the vestibule, so that you may enter the banqueting-hall.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Jacob compares this life to an entry hall whose purpose is preparation for what lies beyond.
judaism.tie_back: Both treat present existence as a passage whose only value is to prepare for release beyond it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares the 'preparatory world' frame; Judaism does not regard the body as excess.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Through many a birth in samsara have I wandered in vain, seeking the builder of this house (of life). Repeated birth is indeed suffering! O house-builder, you are seen! You will not build this house again.”
buddhism.explanation: At his awakening the Buddha declares that he has found craving, the builder of the body-house, and that it will build no more.
buddhism.tie_back: The body is the 'house' that craving keeps rebuilding; for one cutting off births, it is to be ended, not added to.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on ending rebirth and treating embodiment as the product of craving.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Plato reports an Orphic teaching that the body (soma) is the soul's tomb or prison-enclosure (sema), in which the soul pays a penalty until it is released.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Orphic religious tradition, as Plato relays it, saw embodiment as a confinement to be escaped.
greek_mythology.tie_back: If the body itself is a prison, adding further ties is only building more walls — the Kural's reasoning in mythic-religious dress.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the Orphic view is transmitted second-hand and debated by scholars.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedo, Socrates argues that true philosophers practise dying, striving throughout life to separate the soul as far as possible from the body and its demands.
philosophy.explanation: Facing execution, Socrates treats the body as an obstacle to wisdom and philosophy as training for the soul's release.
philosophy.tie_back: For Socrates as for Valluvar, the body is a necessary but excess encumbrance for one seeking release, so nothing further should be added to it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong conceptual match on body as hindrance to the liberated soul.

kurals.tamil:
யானென தென்னுஞ் செருக்கறுப்பான் வானோர்க்
குயர்ந்த உலகம் புகும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Yaanenadhu ennum serukkaruppaan vaanork
kuyarndha ulagam pugum.
kurals.meaning: One who cuts away the pride that says “I” and “mine” will enter a world higher even than the world of the gods.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a kid who stops shouting 'Mine! Mine!' about every toy and stops acting like everything is about them. This kural says a person who drops 'me' and 'mine' reaches a place even better than heaven.
kurals.university: Yaan (“I”) and enadhu (“mine”) are the Tamil counterparts of ahankara and mamakara; Parimelazhagar glosses them as mistaking the body for the self and taking unconnected things as one's own, and calls this pairing serukku — pride or delusion. The reward, vaanorkku uyarndha ulagam (“a world higher than the gods'”), is read by traditional commentators as liberation (veedu), which lies beyond even the heavens, themselves impermanent. Karunanidhi, consistent with his rationalist reading, renders it instead as a renown surpassing heaven's. The couplet thus makes ego itself, not property, the root to be severed — property is simply 'mine' extended outward. The parallel with Gita 2.71 (nirmamo nirahankarah, 'without mine, without ego') is almost verbatim.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A person who has given up all desires for sense gratification, who lives free from desires, who has given up all sense of proprietorship and is devoid of false ego—he alone can attain real peace.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names the pair nirmama (without 'mine') and nirahankara (without 'I') as the conditions for supreme peace.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's yaan/enadhu is the exact Tamil counterpart of the Gita's ahankara/mamata; both promise the highest state to the one who cuts them.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one conceptual and terminological match.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes the death of his old, self-centred ego and its replacement by Christ living within him.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts see the dissolution of the ego-'I' as the doorway to a higher life.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches on the death of the ego; Paul replaces the self with Christ rather than simply extinguishing 'I' and 'mine'.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, "I was only given it because of knowledge I have."”
islam.explanation: Qarun, fabulously rich, credits his wealth to himself; the Quran recounts his arrogance and his destruction.
islam.tie_back: A negative mirror of the Kural: Qarun's 'I' and 'mine' is exactly the pride the Kural says must be cut away.
islam._accuracy_note: Cautionary example rather than direct teaching; no close positive parallel on ego-renunciation leading to a higher world was found in the Quranic text.

judaism.quote_or_event: “be exceeding humble spirit, for the end of man is the worm.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Levitas of Yavneh urges extreme humility, grounded in the reminder of mortality.
judaism.tie_back: Humility here is the Jewish counterpart to cutting off the pride of 'I' and 'mine'.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches on humility; the ground is mortality rather than a promise of a higher realm.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The fool worries, thinking, "I have sons, I have wealth." Indeed, when he himself is not his own, whence are sons, whence is wealth?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha mocks the anxious claim to own sons and wealth, pointing out that the self does not even own itself.
buddhism.tie_back: Both expose the 'I' and the 'mine' as the root delusion; the Buddha adds that the 'I' is not even one's own.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on 'I' and 'mine'; Buddhist anatta goes further than most Kural commentators on the self.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Myth of Er, the soul of Odysseus, cured of ambition by the memory of his former toils, chooses last and searches out the neglected life of a private man with no cares.
greek_mythology.explanation: At the close of the Republic, souls choose their next lives; Odysseus, remembering his past, gladly takes a humble, obscure one.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus's rejection of glory and self-importance is a Greek image of cutting away pride — though in Plato he still returns to earth.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; moderate match on renouncing ambition, but it ends in rebirth rather than liberation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But you, after all, are neither property nor style.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus corrects the reasoning 'I am richer, so I am better', insisting that a person is not identical with what he owns or displays.
philosophy.tie_back: Separating the self from 'mine' is exactly the cut the Kural demands.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches on detaching self from 'mine'; Epictetus does not dissolve the 'I' itself.

kurals.tamil:
பற்றி விடாஅ இடும்பைகள் பற்றினைப்
பற்றி விடாஅ தவர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Patri vidaaa idumbaigal patrinaip
Patri vidaaa thavarkku.
kurals.meaning: Sorrows seize and never let go of those who seize their attachments and will not let them go.
kurals.elementary: If you grab a cactus and refuse to let go, it keeps hurting you. This kural says when you hang on tightly to things, troubles hang on tightly to you.
kurals.university: One of the Kural's most celebrated pieces of wordplay: the phrase patri vidaaa (“seizing, not releasing”) appears twice, first describing sorrows (idumbaigal) and then describing people who hold on to patru (attachment). The mirror structure enacts the moral — the grip we exert is the grip exerted upon us. Mu. Varadarasan specifies the attachments as the twofold 'I' and 'mine' of the previous couplet, making this verse the causal explanation of Kural 346. The same self-reinforcing loop is analysed in Buddhist accounts of craving, in the Gita's chain from dwelling on objects to attachment to desire, and in Spinoza's description of human bondage to the passions.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “While contemplating the objects of the senses, a person develops attachment for them, and from such attachment lust develops, and from lust anger arises.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces a chain reaction: dwelling on objects breeds attachment, attachment breeds desire, and desire breeds anger (and, in the next verse, ruin).
hinduism.tie_back: Both show attachment generating its own suffering in a chain that tightens around the one who clings.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good causal match; the Gita's chain continues in 2.63 to delusion and ruin.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that clinging to wealth traps people in a snare and ends with them piercing themselves with many sorrows.
christianity.tie_back: 'Pierced themselves through with many sorrows' is the Kural's image exactly: the one who clings is held fast by grief of his own making.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on self-inflicted sorrow from clinging, though limited to love of money.

islam.quote_or_event: “Competition in [worldly] increase diverts you Until you visit the graveyards.”
islam.explanation: The Quran describes people so gripped by the race for more that it holds them until death.
islam.tie_back: The grip of acquisitiveness never lets go until the grave — the Kural's picture of attachment holding its holder fast.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches on the relentless hold of worldly striving; the Quran emphasises distraction from God rather than sorrow.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity.”
judaism.explanation: Qoheleth observes that loving wealth produces endless dissatisfaction rather than contentment.
judaism.tie_back: Clinging to wealth produces a restless dissatisfaction that never releases its grip.
judaism._accuracy_note: Partial match: insatiability rather than explicit sorrow.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever is overcome by this wretched and sticky craving, his sorrows grow like grass after the rains.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha calls craving 'sticky' and says the sorrows of one it overcomes multiply like grass after rain.
buddhism.tie_back: 'Sticky' craving and multiplying sorrows mirror the Kural's image of attachment and grief each refusing to let go.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-exact match; verse 336 gives the converse (sorrows fall away like water from a lotus leaf).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Granted his wish that everything he touched should turn to gold, King Midas finds that his food, drink and everything he holds turns to metal, and he begs to be freed from the gift he craved.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid's telling, Midas's greed becomes a curse that clings to his very hands until the god releases him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Midas grasps at gold, and the thing he grasps grasps back — the Kural's 'clinging clings to you' in mythic form.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong narrative illustration of attachment turning into affliction.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza names human weakness in moderating and restraining the emotions 'bondage', explaining that a person ruled by passions is not his own master but is subject to fortune.
philosophy.explanation: In Part IV of the Ethics, Spinoza analyses how passive affects — attachments to external things — hold people captive.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Spinoza sees our attachments as the very chains by which we are held.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics, Part IV, Preface (tr. R. H. M. Elwes)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; Spinoza's remedy is adequate understanding rather than renunciation.

kurals.tamil:
தலைப்பட்டார் தீரத் துறந்தார் மயங்கி
வலைப்பட்டார் மற்றை யவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thalaippattaar theerath thurandhaar mayangi
Valaippattaar matrai yavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who have renounced completely have reached the highest goal; all the others, bewildered, are caught in the net.
kurals.elementary: A fish that swims completely clear of the net stays free, but a fish that stays near it 'just a little' gets caught. This kural says people who give up everything are truly free, while the rest get tangled up.
kurals.university: Theera (“wholly, to the very end”) is the key word: Valluvar contrasts complete renunciants, who have thalaippattaar — 'reached the head', attained the goal — with the rest, who, bewildered (mayangi), are valaippattaar, 'netted'. The rhyming pair thalaippattaar/valaippattaar sharpens the stark binary. Commentators differ over the net: Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah take it as the net of repeated births, Mu. Varadarasan and Karunanidhi as the net of ignorance. The couplet refuses any comfortable middle position — a half-renunciation still counts as capture — in line with Luke 9:62's warning against looking back from the plough and the Gita's 'mesh of delusion'.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Possessed and led astray by such imaginings, enveloped in a mesh of delusion, and addicted to the gratification of sensuous pleasures, they descend to the murkiest hell.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes those driven by endless desires as caught in a 'moha-jala' — a net of delusion — that drags them downward.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita's moha-jala (net of delusion) is precisely the Kural's mayangi valaippattaar, 'bewildered and netted'.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong verbal match on the net of delusion; the Gita's context is 'demoniac' natures rather than incomplete renunciants.

christianity.quote_or_event: “No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus answers a would-be follower who wants first to say goodbye to his family: discipleship admits no looking back.
christianity.tie_back: Both insist that renunciation must be total; divided attention disqualifies.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches on the demand for wholeness; lacks the Kural's net imagery.

islam.quote_or_event: “And what is the life of this world except the enjoyment of delusion.”
islam.explanation: The Quran closes a verse about death and judgment by calling worldly life an enjoyment that deceives.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's 'mayangi' (bewildered) corresponds to the Quran's delusion: those who remain attached to worldly life are deceived by it.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches on the deluding nature of worldly attachment; no explicit total-renunciation ideal.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For man also knoweth not his time: as the fishes that are taken in an evil net, and as the birds that are caught in the snare; so are the sons of men snared in an evil time, when it falleth suddenly upon them.”
judaism.explanation: Qoheleth compares humans to fish and birds suddenly caught in nets and snares.
judaism.tie_back: The same image of human beings caught in a net, though Ecclesiastes speaks of sudden misfortune rather than attachment.
judaism._accuracy_note: Net imagery matches, but the cause is fate/timing, not failure to renounce.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who are lust-infatuated fall back into the swirling current (of samsara) like a spider on its self-spun web. This, too, the wise cut off. Without any longing, they abandon all suffering and renounce the world.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha pictures the passionate as trapped in a web of their own making, while the wise cut it and renounce the world.
buddhism.tie_back: The same two outcomes as the Kural: the renunciants go free; the infatuated remain entangled in a self-spun net.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close match, including the net/web image and the renouncer/infatuated contrast.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hephaestus forges an invisible, unbreakable net and traps Ares and Aphrodite in it in the very act of their illicit passion, exposing them to the laughter of the gods.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the song of Demodocus, the lovers' desire leads them straight into a finely wrought trap.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Those led by desire end up caught in a net — a vivid mythic counterpart to the Kural's valaippattaar.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; net imagery and desire match, but the story is comic and about adultery rather than renunciation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the allegory of the cave, prisoners chained since birth mistake shadows for reality; only one who is freed and turns fully around can climb out to the sunlight.
philosophy.explanation: Plato depicts ordinary human life as bondage to illusion, from which only a complete turning of the soul releases one.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato's chained, deluded prisoners correspond to the Kural's 'bewildered, netted' majority; the freed philosopher to the one who has reached the height.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the cave concerns ignorance more than attachment, though Plato links the two.

kurals.tamil:
பற்றற்ற கண்ணே பிறப்பறுக்கும் மற்று
நிலையாமை காணப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Patratra kanne pirapparukkum matru
Nilaiyaamai kaanap padum.
kurals.meaning: At the very moment attachment ceases, the cycle of birth is cut; otherwise, instability — the endless round of coming and going — is what will be seen.
kurals.elementary: A spinning top keeps going as long as you keep flicking it; stop flicking, and it finally rests. This kural says once you stop clinging, the cycle of being born again and again stops — and if you don't, everything keeps wobbling and changing.
kurals.university: Kanne (“at that very point”) stresses immediacy: liberation coincides with the cessation of patru rather than following it as a later reward. The second line is read in two ways. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan take matru as 'otherwise': without detachment, instability — the alternation of births and deaths — will be seen. Puliyur Kesikan reads it as 'moreover': with detachment, the impermanence of the world is then clearly seen. Either way the couplet binds this chapter to the preceding one, Nilaiyaamai (Impermanence, ch. 34). The claim that the end of desire is the end of rebirth is shared almost word for word by the Katha Upanishad and the Dhammapada, and appears inverted in the Orphic hope of escaping the 'wheel'.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When all desires that dwell in his heart cease, then the mortal becomes immortal, and obtains Brahman.”
hinduism.explanation: Death himself (Yama) teaches Nachiketas that the cessation of all desires is the moment the mortal becomes immortal.
hinduism.tie_back: Same claim and same immediacy as the Kural: when attachment ends, birth-and-death ends.
hinduism.source: Katha Upanishad II.6.14 (2.3.14) (tr. F. Max Müller, SBE vol. 15)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; the following verse adds 'when all the ties of the heart are severed here on earth'.

christianity.quote_or_event: “While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.”
christianity.explanation: Paul directs believers' attention away from visible, temporary things to invisible, eternal ones.
christianity.tie_back: Both contrast the instability of what is clung to with the permanence gained by looking beyond it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches on impermanence vs. the eternal; no rebirth doctrine in Christianity.

islam.quote_or_event: “And present to them the example of the life of this world, [its being] like rain which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it and [then] it becomes dry remnants, scattered by the winds.”
islam.explanation: The Quran likens worldly life to vegetation that flourishes after rain and is soon blown away as dry debris.
islam.tie_back: The instability (nilaiyaamai) the Kural says is seen by those still attached is here pictured as vegetation scattered by the wind.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the impermanence strand only; Islam has no rebirth cycle to be cut.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.”
judaism.explanation: Qoheleth opens by declaring all worldly striving to be hevel — vapour, fleeting breath.
judaism.tie_back: The same insight into the instability of everything grasped, without the Kural's promise of release.
judaism._accuracy_note: Weak-to-moderate: shares the impermanence theme, but Judaism has no doctrine of cutting off rebirth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let go of the past, let go of the future, let go of the present, and cross over to the farther shore of existence. With mind wholly liberated, you shall come no more to birth and death.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges total letting-go and promises that the wholly liberated mind will not return to birth and death.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's claim: complete release from clinging ends the cycle of birth.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-exact match on detachment ending rebirth.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On gold tablets buried with Orphic initiates, the soul declares to the underworld powers that it has flown out of the grievous, weary circle (or wheel) of existence and asks to be admitted among the blessed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Orphic initiates hoped to escape a cycle of reincarnation through purification and ritual.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Orphic 'wheel' is the Greek counterpart to the cycle of births the Kural says is cut when attachment ends.
greek_mythology.source: Orphic gold tablet from Thurii (4th century BCE)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the tablets' wording varies and their interpretation is debated; the means of release is ritual purity rather than detachment.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Consolation of Philosophy, Lady Philosophy shows Boethius that Fortune turns her wheel ceaselessly, so anyone who ties his happiness to her gifts must expect to be thrown down.
philosophy.explanation: Imprisoned and ruined, Boethius learns that clinging to the goods of Fortune binds one to her endless instability.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's 'otherwise, instability is seen', Boethius shows attachment to worldly goods locking one into perpetual change.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; matches the instability strand only, not the ending of rebirth.

kurals.tamil:
பற்றுக பற்றற்றான் பற்றினை அப்பற்றைப்
பற்றுக பற்று விடற்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Patruga patratraan patrinai appatraip
Patruga patru vidarku.
kurals.meaning: Hold fast to the One who is free of all attachment; hold fast to that attachment alone, so that you can let go of every other.
kurals.elementary: When you're learning to swim, you hold on to the edge of the pool so you can stop being scared of the water. This kural says hold on to God — the one who clings to nothing — so you can let go of everything else.
kurals.university: The chapter's closing couplet repeats forms of patru (“attachment, clinging”) six times, a virtuoso climax. It resolves a paradox the chapter has built up: desire cannot simply be willed away, so Valluvar prescribes a single counter-attachment — to patratraan, 'the One without attachment', whom Parimelazhagar and most commentators identify as God, whose feet are to be held — as the instrument for dropping all other attachments. Karunanidhi, in keeping with his secular reading, takes patratraan to mean any truly detached person, making the verse a counsel to cling to the company of the detached. The strategy of replacing a lower attachment with a higher one parallels the Gita's 'higher taste', while the Buddha's raft simile adds the caution that even the means is finally to be let go.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The embodied soul may be restricted from sense enjoyment, though the taste for sense objects remains. But, ceasing such engagements by experiencing a higher taste, he is fixed in consciousness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna notes that forced abstinence leaves the craving intact; only the experience of something higher makes the lower taste fall away.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita's 'higher taste' is the Kural's strategy exactly: cling to the higher attachment in order to release the lower ones.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong structural match (higher attachment dissolves lower); the Gita verse does not explicitly name God, though the purport does.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that holding on to Christ has made everything else he once valued worthless by comparison.
christianity.tie_back: Clinging to Christ is what enables Paul to let go of everything else — the Kural's single, liberating attachment.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good structural match; Christianity describes God as loving rather than 'without attachment'.

islam.quote_or_event: “And remember the name of your Lord and devote yourself to Him with [complete] devotion.”
islam.explanation: The Arabic 'tabattal ilayhi tabtila' literally suggests cutting oneself off from all else in order to devote oneself wholly to God.
islam.tie_back: Tabattul — severing from everything to cleave to God alone — is the Kural's formula of one attachment used to cut all others.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match via the root sense of tabattul; the English translation softens the 'cutting off' nuance.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee. My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist declares that God is his only desire and his lasting portion, even as everything else fails.
judaism.tie_back: A single, all-absorbing attachment to God that renders every other desire unnecessary — the heart of the Kural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong devotional match; the psalm does not frame it as a technique for releasing other attachments.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the same way, monks, I have taught the Dhamma compared to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of holding onto.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares his teaching to a raft: something to hold on to while crossing the flood, and then to leave behind.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's single permitted attachment, the Dhamma is grasped as a means to let go — though the Buddha adds that even it must finally be released.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on 'use an attachment to cross beyond attachment'; Buddhism has no personal deity in the Kural's sense.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When his raft is sucked into Charybdis, Odysseus leaps up and clings to a fig tree growing over the whirlpool, holding on until the wreckage is thrown back up and he can escape.
greek_mythology.explanation: Everything else is swallowed by the whirlpool; holding one fixed point is what saves him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A loose image of the Kural's counsel: amid the whirlpool, cling to the one stable thing in order to be freed from everything else.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak, analogical match only; no Greek myth closely parallels clinging to a detached deity to release attachments.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plotinus ends the Enneads by describing the soul's ascent as a withdrawal from all things of this world toward the One, famously characterised as the flight of the alone to the Alone.
philosophy.explanation: For Plotinus, the soul must turn away from multiplicity and cleave to the One, which is itself beyond need and attachment.
philosophy.tie_back: Clinging to the One that clings to nothing, in order to shed every lower tie, is close to the Kural's paradox.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good structural match, though Plotinian union is contemplative rather than devotional.

ovid-midas.title: Ovid, Metamorphoses Book 11 (Midas and the golden touch)
